subject: Banking
title: Japan's Lost Decade Banking Crisis
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Japan's Lost Decade Banking Crisis.

hook.text: Japan's real estate bubble burst in 1990. Banks held trillions in bad loans but hid them for a decade.

buildup.text: At the peak, Tokyo's Imperial Palace grounds were worth more than all California real estate. Then prices collapsed 80%.

discovery.text: Japanese banks practiced 'extend and pretend.' They renewed bad loans instead of writing them off.

twist.text: Japan's GDP stayed near zero for two decades. The banking system's refusal to recognize losses froze the economy.

climax.text: Japan proved that hiding banking losses delays recovery.

punchline.text: Hide the losses. Fund the zombies. Japan's economy froze for 20 years.

quiz.question: What are 'zombie banks'?
options: Banks that keep renewing bad loans instead of recognizing losses

details.summary: Japan's banking crisis began when a massive asset bubble burst in 1990, leaving banks with trillions in bad loans they refused to write off. The resulting zombie banking system contributed to two decades of economic stagnation.
details.whyItMatters: Japan's lost decades demonstrate the catastrophic cost of allowing zombie banks to persist. Delaying write-offs and reforms turned what could have been a sharp recession into a generation of economic malaise.
takeaways: Japanese bank losses from the bubble exceeded $1 trillion
Banks kept lending to insolvent companies to avoid recognizing losses
Japan's GDP growth averaged under 1 percent for over two decades

faq.question: What are zombie banks and why are they dangerous?
faq.answer: Zombie banks are institutions kept alive with hidden losses on their books. They continue operating but cannot lend productively because their capital is consumed by bad loans they refuse to acknowledge. They crowd out healthy competitors.

faq.question: What lessons does Japan's crisis offer other countries?
faq.answer: The key lesson is to recognize losses quickly, recapitalize or close failed banks promptly, and avoid prolonging the pain through denial. The US applied these lessons in 2008 by stress testing banks and forcing rapid recapitalization.
